content:
Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's 20th anniversary iPhone, which is said to embody Apple's long-standing vision of "a single slab of glass."

There have already been conflicting reports about what exactly to expect, but yesterday's divergence was the biggest so far...

The current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive often spoke of his long-term vision for the iPhone, which was that it would eventually become a single piece of glass. It is widely believed that, even after Ive's departure, Apple still holds to this vision.

Although Apple doesn't generally make a big fuss about product anniversaries, the mainstream view is that they are aiming to realise this vision as much as possible for the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This is likely to include embedding Face ID under the display, and possibly hiding the front-facing camera under the screen as well.

However, we have already seen many conflicting reports. Although the initial assumption was that it would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, more recent reports suggest that this design will instead be used on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In sequence, that should be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may skip that name to celebrate the anniversary and jump straight to the iPhone 20.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Things got even more confusing yesterday, when an analyst claimed that Apple had abandoned the idea of launching an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately stepped in to rebut that claim.

The more likely reality

The key point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone is not a single endpoint. Whatever Apple plans to launch next year will be just one or more steps towards that sci-fi vision of "a single slab of glass."

The question is not whether that goal will be reached next year, but how far Apple will go towards that vision. But whether it's one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in the evolution of the iPhone's design.

In fact, Gurman says Apple has already compromised on what it had originally hoped to achieve by next year.

The Jefferies analyst likely heard the same thing, but heard it closer to the source, and took it to mean that Apple had completely abandoned the plan.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a significant step forward—the equivalent of the leap made with the iPhone X—but that there will be further developments in the years to come. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will advance enough for Apple to apply some special branding, whether that means labelling it a 20th anniversary iPhone (which seems unlikely to me), using some other special name, or skipping a generation and calling it the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
